presidents.name: Andrew Jackson
presidents.summary: Andrew Jackson enslaved people throughout his adult life at the Hermitage in Tennessee and at properties in several other states. As president he asked Congress to criminalize the mailing of antislavery material into the South, and the House adopted its first gag rule on antislavery petitions in the last full year of his second term.
presidents.paragraph: Jackson bought his first enslaved person, a woman named Nancy, in 1788, and the Hermitage records the count rising from ten people when he moved there in 1804 to ninety-five when he was elected in 1828 and about a hundred and fifty when he died in 1845. The Miller Center's biographical essay says he grew up with slavery and accepted it uncritically, buying and selling people and using them to work his plantation. The political side shows up in 1835, when abolitionists mailed thousands of antislavery tracts to southern addresses and postmasters and mobs stopped many of them. In his December 1835 annual message Jackson asked Congress for a law that would prohibit, under severe penalties, circulating incendiary publications through the southern mails. He didn't get that statute, but the House went its own way: on May 26, 1836, it adopted Henry Pinckney's resolution automatically tabling every petition touching slavery, over John Quincy Adams's objection that it violated the Constitution.

presidents.personalRecord: Jackson enslaved people from 1788 until his death. The Hermitage documents his first purchase (a woman named Nancy, 1788), ten enslaved people in 1804, 95 at his 1828 election, and about 150 inherited by his son at his death in 1845; the site states the Jackson family enslaved at least 325 people over 77 years, and researchers have identified more than 500 names of people enslaved there or their descendants. He freed no one at his death. The Miller Center records that he bought and sold people and never treated slavery as a moral question.

presidents.name: Martin Van Buren
presidents.summary: Martin Van Buren campaigned in 1836 and pledged in his 1837 inaugural address to oppose any congressional attempt to abolish slavery in the District of Columbia and to resist interference with slavery in the states. His administration argued in court that the Africans who seized the schooner Amistad should be returned to their claimed Spanish owners, and the Supreme Court ruled against the government in 1841.
presidents.paragraph: Van Buren grew up around slavery in Kinderhook, New York, where his father Abraham enslaved six people, and a letter in his own papers shows he had enslaved a man named Tom who left him around the 1810s. As a candidate he committed himself in writing, then repeated the pledge word for word in his March 1837 inaugural address: he would be the inflexible and uncompromising opponent of any attempt by Congress to abolish slavery in the District of Columbia, and would resist the slightest interference with it in the states, adding that no bill conflicting with those views could ever get his signature. The Amistad case ran through his whole second half of the term. His administration treated the captive Africans as property and pressed for their return, and in January 1840 he issued an executive order to hand them over. The Supreme Court decided otherwise in 1841, ordering that they be declared free and dismissed from custody.

presidents.personalRecord: Van Buren's father Abraham enslaved six people in Kinderhook, New York, making him one of that town's larger slaveholders under the 1790 census. An 1824 letter in Van Buren's own papers at the Library of Congress, from Alonzo G. Hammond, refers to 'Tom,' a Black man Hammond says Van Buren purchased and who had left him roughly ten years earlier; Van Buren's shorthand note on it reads that if Tom could be gotten without violence he would take $50. New York's gradual emancipation freed Tom's class on July 4, 1827. No figure for enslaved people held by Van Buren at his death was verified here.

presidents.name: William Henry Harrison
presidents.summary: William Henry Harrison died one month after taking the oath of office, so he has no presidential record on slavery beyond his inaugural address. His documented record is earlier: as governor of Indiana Territory he called the 1802 Vincennes convention that petitioned Congress to suspend the Northwest Ordinance's ban on slavery, and in 1805 he approved a territorial indenture act that let slaveholders bring enslaved people in as indentured servants.
presidents.paragraph: Harrison's presidency lasted one month, so the substance is in his territorial career. On November 22, 1802 he issued a proclamation calling a general convention at Vincennes to consider repealing the sixth article of compact, the clause of the Northwest Ordinance that barred slavery. The convention's December petition asked Congress to suspend the article for ten years and to let people brought in during that window stay enslaved afterward. Congress said no, and kept saying no. In 1805 the territory's first assembly passed, and Harrison approved on August 26, an act letting anyone who held or purchased enslaved people anywhere in the United States bring them into the territory and indenture them, with terms set by the holder for people over fifteen and fixed ages for children. The Indiana Historical Bureau describes Harrison as a slaveholder who encouraged slavery in Indiana. His 1841 inaugural argued that residents of the District of Columbia were free American citizens, not subjects.

presidents.name: John Tyler
presidents.summary: John Tyler enslaved people on Virginia plantations he inherited and built, and brought enslaved workers into the White House. He drove the annexation of Texas as a slaveholding state, signing the joint resolution on March 1, 1845, three days before leaving office, and two decades later was elected to the Confederate House of Representatives.
presidents.paragraph: Tyler inherited Greenway and thirteen enslaved people from his father in 1813, then built his own plantation, Woodburn; the 1820 census counted twenty-four enslaved people there and by 1830 twenty-nine, more than half of them under ten years old. In office he pushed hard for Texas. His Secretary of State John C. Calhoun tied annexation openly to the defense of slavery, and when the treaty route failed Tyler switched to a joint resolution needing only simple majorities in both chambers. It passed, and he signed it into law on March 1, 1845, three days before his term ended. One man enslaved in his household, James Hambleton Christian, later escaped and told his story to William Still, who published it in The Underground Rail Road. In 1861 Tyler chaired a failed peace convention, then backed secession and was elected to the Confederate House of Representatives, dying before it first met.

presidents.name: James K. Polk
presidents.summary: James K. Polk owned plantations in Tennessee and Mississippi and used enslaved labor in the White House. While president he secretly bought nineteen more enslaved people through agents, at least thirteen of them children, and opposed the Wilmot Proviso's ban on slavery in territory taken from Mexico, favoring instead extension of the Missouri Compromise line to the Pacific.
presidents.paragraph: Polk's father died in 1827 leaving 8,000 acres and fifty-three enslaved people to be divided among his widow and ten children. Polk built his own operation, moving enslaved people from Somerville to a plantation near Yalobusha, Mississippi, partly because he thought escape would be harder farther south, and keeping them in the dark about the move. As president he used plantation profits to buy nineteen more people through agents in Tennessee, instructing his cousin Robert Campbell that the purchases should not be known to anyone else. At least thirteen of the nineteen were children, some as young as twelve, bought away from their families. On policy, the Wilmot Proviso arrived in August 1846 proposing that neither slavery nor involuntary servitude ever exist in territory acquired from Mexico. Polk opposed it and pushed instead to extend the old Missouri Compromise line of 36°30' to the Pacific. He drafted veto language warning that liberty's blessings could be lost forever.

presidents.personalRecord: Polk enslaved people from young adulthood until his death in June 1849. His father Samuel left 8,000 acres and fifty-three enslaved people to his widow and ten children in 1827. Polk ran plantations in Tennessee and Mississippi, used enslaved labor in the White House, and bought nineteen more people during his presidency, at least thirteen of them children. The White House Historical Association concludes he 'was a profit-hungry slave owner, ripping apart families for his own personal gain.' Purchases begun in his final weeks in office were finalized after he left Washington. A precise count enslaved at his death was not verified here.

presidents.name: Zachary Taylor
presidents.summary: Zachary Taylor was a career soldier and Mississippi and Louisiana planter who enslaved well over a hundred people while serving as president. He urged California and New Mexico to write constitutions and seek statehood directly, bypassing a congressional bargain over slavery, and he opposed Henry Clay's compromise measures until his death on July 9, 1850.
presidents.paragraph: Taylor grew up on his father's Kentucky plantation and inherited two enslaved men, Charles and Tom, in 1829; they stayed with him until he died. In 1842 he bought Cypress Grove plantation in Rodney, Mississippi, and with it eighty-one enslaved men, women, and children whose names the deed records, on top of holdings he already had in Mississippi and Louisiana. He bought sixty-four more before his death. He also brought enslaved people to the White House. On policy he went a different direction from most southern politicians: in his December 1849 annual message he told Congress the people of California had met in convention to form a state government and would shortly apply for admission, and he pressed for statehood without a congressional deal on slavery. He opposed Clay's compromise. He died July 9, 1850, and his will left roughly 131 people to his family as slaves for life.

presidents.personalRecord: Taylor enslaved people continuously as an adult. He inherited two enslaved men, Charles and Tom, from his father in 1829, and they remained with him until his death in 1850. In 1842 he bought Cypress Grove plantation with eighty-one enslaved people, already holding others in Mississippi and Baton Rouge, Louisiana, and bought sixty-four more before he died. Enslaved people worked in his White House; a man named Porter died at the Executive Mansion in 1849. His will left approximately 131 people to his wife and three children as 'slaves for life' and freed none.

disputes: Taylor and the Wilmot Proviso: the White House Historical Association says he 'vacillated' on supporting it, and notes that Southern Whigs expected a veto while Northern Whigs believed he might quietly support it. The Miller Center presents him as expecting free-state constitutions from California and New Mexico. Both are recorded.

How antislavery Taylor was: contemporaries called him more antislavery than most southern politicians because he opposed extension, while abolitionists in 1848 attacked him precisely as a slaveholder. Both characterizations appear in the fetched sources.
unverified: Whether Taylor ever stated he would veto the Compromise of 1850 measures outright, as opposed to opposing them.
